result.markdown: --- title: "Session 2 — Ordinal Logistic Regression" subtitle: "Proportional odds · cumulative logits · odds ratios · thresholds · predicted probabilities · Lab 2" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Session 1: ordered vs nominal outcomes; cumulative proportions - Today: the **proportional-odds model** for an ordered outcome - By the end you can: - fit it with `MASS::polr` and read **odds ratios** - explain the **thresholds** - give **predicted probabilities** for each category ::: # Topic 1 — The model {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Cumulative logits ::: {.eq} logit P(Y ≤ k) = ζ~k~ − (β~1~x~1~ + β~2~x~2~ + …) k = 1, 2, 3 ::: ::: {.incremental} - One **threshold** ζ~k~ for each cut-point between categories (3 for 4 categories) - **One set of coefficients** β shared by all cut-points: the **proportional-odds** (parallel lines) assumption - exp(β) is the **odds ratio for being in a higher category**: the same whichever cut-point you look at - In `polr`, β > 0 means **higher categories** (worse anaemia) are more likely ::: ## One predictor ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m1 <- MASS::polr(anaemia ~ wealth, data = mat, Hess = TRUE) round(exp(cbind(OR = coef(m1), confint(m1))), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` OR 2.5 % 0.57 0.53 97.5 % 0.57 0.63 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} m1$zeta |> round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` None|Mild Mild|Moderate Moderate|Severe -1.39 0.00 1.21 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} **OR = 0.57 per wealth quintile**: each quintile higher multiplies the **odds of being in a worse anaemia category** by about 0.57 (a **43% reduction**), **at every cut-point** (None vs worse, up to Moderate vs Severe). ::: # Topic 2 — An adjusted model {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Several predictors ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m2 <- MASS::polr(anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + tribal + residence, data = mat, Hess = TRUE) round(exp(cbind(OR = coef(m2), confint(m2))), 2) # tbl_regression(m2, exponentiate = TRUE) formats this for a paper ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` OR 2.5 % 97.5 % wealth 0.76 0.68 0.85 educationPrimary 0.75 0.57 0.99 educationSecondary 0.62 0.45 0.86 educationHigher 0.46 0.31 0.66 bmi 0.93 0.90 0.96 anc_visits 0.90 0.84 0.95 parity 1.11 1.01 1.21 age 1.01 1.00 1.03 tribalYes 1.11 0.83 1.48 residenceRural 1.21 0.94 1.56 ``` ::: ::: ## Reading the adjusted odds ratios ::: {.incremental} - **Wealth, higher education, BMI and antenatal visits** are protective (OR below 1) - **Parity** goes slightly the other way - The OR for **tribal group** is only about 1.1: **do not trust it yet**. Session 3 shows the model is wrong for that variable - `confint()` gives profile-likelihood CIs; p-values come from the t value (|t| above about 2) ::: ## Thresholds ::: {.eq} None|Mild: ζ~1~ Mild|Moderate: ζ~2~ Moderate|Severe: ζ~3~ ::: They are the **baseline log-odds** of each cumulative probability (when all predictors are 0) and are **not** of substantive interest. **K categories need K − 1 thresholds.** # Topic 3 — Predicted probabilities {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## What it means for a woman ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nd <- data.frame(wealth = c(1, 5), education = factor("Primary", levels = levels(mat$education)), bmi = 20.5, anc_visits = 3, parity = 2, age = 27, tribal = factor("No", levels = c("No", "Yes")), residence = factor("Rural", levels = c("Urban", "Rural"))) rownames(nd) <- c("poorest", "richest") round(predict(m2, newdata = nd, type = "probs"), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` None Mild Moderate Severe poorest 0.38 0.34 0.18 0.10 richest 0.65 0.24 0.08 0.03 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Probability of **each** category for a given profile: the four numbers add to 1 - The **poorest** woman has about a **10% chance of severe anaemia**; the **richest** about **3%** - Clearer for readers than odds ratios: report **both** ::: ## Compared with a binary model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(ordinal = unname(exp(coef(m1))), binary_any_vs_none = unname(exp(coef(glm(I(anaemia != "None") ~ wealth, family = binomial, data = mat)))["wealth"])) |> round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ordinal binary_any_vs_none 0.57 0.57 ``` ::: ::: When proportional odds holds, the ordinal and the binary ORs agree, but the **ordinal model uses the severity too**, so it is **more precise**. ## Reporting an ordinal model ::: {.good} - State the **outcome order** and the **model** (cumulative-logit, proportional odds) - **Odds ratios** with CIs, and say they are for **a higher category** - A few **predicted probabilities** - The **assumption check** (next session) ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 2 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `ordinal-workshop/labs/lab2_ordinal.R` - `MASS::polr()` unadjusted and adjusted - odds ratios, thresholds, `tbl_regression` - predicted probabilities and a binary comparison ::: **Time:** 35 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s2q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="eyk5wx.mugnt2" data-show="RWFjaCBxdWludGlsZSBoaWdoZXIgbXVsdGlwbGllcyB0aGUgb2RkcyBvZiBhIHdvcnNlIGNh dGVnb3J5IGJ5IDAuNTc=" data-explain="VGhlIE9SIGNvbXBhcmVzIG9kZHMgb2YgYmVpbmcgaW4gYSBoaWdoZXIgY2F0ZWdvcnkgdmVy c3VzIGxvd2VyIG9uZXMsIGFuZCB1bmRlciBwcm9wb3J0aW9uYWwgb2RkcyBpdCBpcyB0aGUg c2FtZSBhdCBldmVyeSBjdXQtcG9pbnQu"} A proportional-odds model gives OR = 0.57 per wealth quintile. Which is the best reading? - Each quintile higher lowers the anaemia grade by 0.57 categories on average - Women in the top quintile have 57% of the anaemia of the poorest women - Each quintile higher multiplies the odds of a worse category by 0.57 - The probability of anaemia is 0.57 for each one of the quintiles ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s2q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="eykj5l.muh2ae" data-show="VGhlcmUgYXJlIHRocmVlIGN1dC1wb2ludHMgYmV0d2VlbiBmb3VyIG9yZGVyZWQgY2F0ZWdv cmllcw==" data-explain="QSBLLWNhdGVnb3J5IG91dGNvbWUgaGFzIEsgLSAxIGN1bXVsYXRpdmUgcHJvYmFiaWxpdGll cywgc28gSyAtIDEgdGhyZXNob2xkcyAoaW50ZXJjZXB0cyku"} Why does a model for a four-category outcome have three thresholds? - Three of the four categories are used up as references - There are three cut-points between four ordered categories - The model needs one separate threshold for each predictor - Four categories need four thresholds minus one for the intercept ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s2q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="eykweb.muhgrs" data-show="RWFjaCBwcmVkaWN0b3IncyBlZmZlY3QgaXMgdGhlIHNhbWUgYXQgZXZlcnkgY3V0LXBvaW50 IG9mIHRoZSBvdXRjb21l" data-explain="T25lIHNldCBvZiBjb2VmZmljaWVudHMgYXBwbGllcyB0byBhbGwgY3VtdWxhdGl2ZSBsb2dp dHMsIHNvIGVhY2ggb2RkcyByYXRpbyBpcyBjb25zdGFudCBhY3Jvc3MgY3V0LXBvaW50cy4g RXF1YWwgc3BhY2luZyBpcyBub3QgYXNzdW1lZC4="} What is the proportional-odds assumption? - The categories of the outcome are equally spaced in terms of severity - The predictors are proportional to the outcome on the log-odds scale - Each predictor's effect is the same at every cut-point of the outcome - The odds of each single category are equal in all of the groups ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s2q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="eyl9n1.muhv96" data-show="VGhleSBnaXZlIHRoZSBjaGFuY2Ugb2YgZWFjaCBjYXRlZ29yeSBvbiBhIHNjYWxlIHJlYWRl cnMgdW5kZXJzdGFuZA==" data-explain="T2RkcyByYXRpb3MgYXJlIG9uIGEgbG9nLW9kZHMgc2NhbGUgdGhhdCBpcyBoYXJkIHRvIGdy YXNwOyBwcmVkaWN0ZWQgcHJvYmFiaWxpdGllcyBzaG93IHdoYXQgdGhlIG1vZGVsIGltcGxp ZXMgZm9yIGEgd29tYW4gd2l0aCBhIGdpdmVuIHByb2ZpbGUu"} Why are predicted probabilities useful alongside odds ratios? - They are always more accurate than the odds ratios from the same model - They remove the need to check the model assumptions of the analysis - They show whether each of the thresholds is significant or not - They give the chance of each category on a scale readers understand ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s2q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="eylmvn.mui9qg" data-show="SGlnaGVyIHZhbHVlcyBtYWtlIHRoZSBoaWdoZXIgKHdvcnNlKSBjYXRlZ29yaWVzIG1vcmUg bGlrZWx5" data-explain="SW4gdGhlIHVzdWFsIHBvbHIgcGFyYW1ldHJpc2F0aW9uLCBwb3NpdGl2ZSBjb2VmZmljaWVu dHMgbW92ZSB0aGUgcHJvYmFiaWxpdHkgdXAgdGhlIG9yZGVyZWQgc2NhbGUsIHRvd2FyZHMg dGhlIGxhc3QgY2F0ZWdvcnku"} In polr, a positive coefficient for a predictor means what? - Higher values make the higher (worse) categories more likely - Higher values make the lower categories more likely to be seen - The predictor is significant at the 5% level in the sample - The predictor reduces all of the thresholds to exactly zero ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - **Proportional-odds**: one OR per predictor, the same at every cut-point - exp(β) = odds of a **higher category**; K categories → **K − 1 thresholds** - Report **ORs with CI** and **predicted probabilities** - The single OR is only trustworthy if the **assumption holds** ::: **Next:** Session 3: checking proportional odds

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
